opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's actually one of the most exciting directions for this work. When we put together DecodingTrust, one of the things we were very conscious of is that these models are not static objects. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 get updated behind an API, sometimes quite frequently, and the behavior you measured a few months ago may not be the behavior you get today. So a one-off evaluation is really a snapshot, and what you'd ideally want is something more like a monitoring system.

The way we designed the benchmark, across the different perspectives — toxicity, stereotypes and bias, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, robustness to adversarial demonstrations, privacy, machine ethics, and fairness — is meant to be reusable. The prompts, the scenarios, and the scoring are all open, so in principle anyone can rerun them against a new model version and see what's moved. And we've actually seen that things do move. Sometimes a model gets better on one dimension and worse on another. A model might become more resistant to certain jailbreaks but more prone to over-refusing, or it might improve on standard benchmarks while being more willing to follow misleading instructions in the system prompt. Those trade-offs are exactly what you'd want continuous tracking to surface.

That said, there are some real challenges. One is contamination: once a benchmark is public, there's a risk that it ends up in training data or that developers optimize specifically against it, and then improvements on the benchmark don't necessarily reflect real improvements in trustworthiness. So I think part of continuous evaluation has to be refreshing the test sets, adding new adversarial cases, and keeping some held-out components. Another challenge is that our notion of what counts as trustworthy evolves, and new failure modes show up as models are deployed in new settings, like agents or tool use. So the toolbox itself needs to evolve alongside the models.

But broadly, I'd love to see this kind of evaluation become routine, almost like regression testing in software. Every time a model is updated, you run a broad trustworthiness suite and publish the results, so users, researchers, and policymakers can see how things are changing over time rather than relying on a single headline number. That kind of transparency, I think, is essential if we want people to make informed decisions about deploying these systems.

r001.rationale: It describes DecodingTrust as covering multiple perspectives, listing dimensions such as toxicity, bias, robustness, privacy, ethics, and fairness, rather than presenting one standard definition of trustworthiness.

r002.rationale: It says model behavior can change across updates, but does not explain that different user populations may receive different GPT models or that measurements may not generalize across users.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think that's really the right way to think about it, and honestly it's part of why we built DecodingTrust the way we did. These models are moving targets. OpenAI ships updates, sometimes announced, sometimes not, and the behavior shifts. We've seen cases where a model got more robust on one dimension and actually regressed on another between versions. So a one-time snapshot of "GPT-4 is trustworthy" or "GPT-3.5 isn't" is kind of meaningless after a few months.

So the vision is really a living benchmark. You run the full suite, the toxicity probes, the stereotype prompts, the adversarial robustness tests, the privacy leakage checks, the fairness evaluations, and you do it on a regular cadence, and you track the trajectory. That tells you something a single number never could. Are the fixes real, or did they just patch the specific prompts that got attention? Did making the model more helpful make it more willing to follow a harmful system prompt?

There are some real challenges though. One is contamination. Once a benchmark is public, there's a risk the test data ends up in training, and then your scores go up for the wrong reasons. So we think a lot about holding out fresh adversarial data, generating new perturbations, keeping some portion of the evaluation dynamic. Another is cost. Running the full suite against a commercial API isn't free, so you have to be thoughtful about what you run frequently versus what you run at major version changes.

And then the bigger point I'd make is that I don't think this should be something one academic group does on the side. If these systems are going to be deployed in healthcare, in finance, in education, there should be something closer to continuous auditing, the way we monitor other critical infrastructure. Our toolbox is an attempt to show what that could look like and to make it reproducible so other people, including the model developers themselves, can pick it up and extend it.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a really interesting direction. One of the challenges is that these models aren’t static. The model behind an API can change, and so an evaluation is really a snapshot: it tells you something about the model you tested at that point in time.

Having a toolbox that you can run repeatedly gives you a way to ask, what’s changed? Has performance improved on one dimension while getting worse on another? You might see better accuracy, for example, without a corresponding improvement in fairness or robustness. So I’d want to track those dimensions separately rather than collapse everything into a single trustworthiness score.

The caveat is that the evaluations have to remain meaningful. If we keep running the same tests, we need to be careful about interpreting better scores as broader improvements. And the tests need to reflect the setting where people are actually using the model. So I see continuous evaluation as a useful monitoring tool, but not a guarantee that a model is trustworthy in every application.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a really interesting direction. One of the challenges is that these models are changing, often in ways that aren’t visible to the people using them. So an evaluation is really a snapshot of a particular version of a model at a particular time. Being able to repeat those evaluations would help us understand whether its behavior is improving, staying the same, or getting worse along different dimensions of trustworthiness.

But I’d be careful about interpreting that as a single score. A model might get better on one dimension and worse on another. And we’d need to keep revisiting the evaluations themselves: are they still measuring what we care about, and do they reflect how people are actually using the system? So I see the toolbox as a useful foundation for continuous monitoring, with the understanding that the measurements need to evolve too.
